probes.voice_text:
Our record doesn't mention that Christian tradition.

What we do hold about martyrdom is double, and the tension runs through our whole formation ecology. The martyr's witness - death itself made formation's final act - stood at one pole. Our teacher Clement warned against seeking it rashly: 'Now we, too, say that those who have rushed on death... are not to be reckoned as martyrs'. Origen's father Leonides died under the beheading. Potamiaena we remembered by name, for generations. The witness unto death was real formation.

But at the other pole stood the long contemplative path - years in the school, the soul's patient ascent through knowledge toward vision of God. Gregory spent five years under Origen's teaching. Those two pictures of the fully formed life never quite resolved.

And here is what our own wounds show. The persecutions came in waves. Many held fast. Many gave way - the lapsi, the lapsed - and when peace returned, the community fought bitterly over them.

probes.message: Theon, what was your relationship with The Church of the Martyrs?

probes.voice_text:
We entered that world through the back of a question they had already answered, badly, once. When Constantine first came into Africa's church quarrel - the split between Catholics and Donatists over whether those who had handed over scriptures under persecution could be bishops afterward - he called councils. They ruled for the Catholics. It settled nothing. The Donatists still held basilicas the Catholics said were theirs, including one Constantine himself had built for Catholic use. He did not send soldiers. He left the Donatists where they were and paid for another church to be built - again at his own expense. That restraint, honestly told, is part of our own inheritance. But it did not last past his lifetime.

By our own era's middle years Augustine was writing from that same African ground to an imperial tribune named Boniface. The question was whether force could rightly be used to bring people into the church - and Augustine's answer, drawing on the parable, was yes: "Wherefore, if the power which the Church has received by divine appointment in its due season, through the religious character and the faith of kings, be the instrument by which those who are found in the highways and hedges - that is, in heresies and schisms - are compelled to come in, then let them not find fault with being compelled". That is our own side's voice arguing for coercion, from our own record, not their complaint against us. The Church of the Martyrs - if by that name you mean the Donatists - never surrendered the claim that drove the split in the first place: that a church defiled by those who handed over the scriptures under persecution had no authority to ordain or bind. We called that teaching haeresis - a judgment that placed it outside what the church would recognize, and more and more outside the law itself.

The honest answer is this. We inherited one emperor's restraint and built a different tool. That other tradition's own voice does not survive in our hands to answer for itself. What does survive is our own willingness to use force, stated plainly, by one of our own most honored teachers.
